Title: Christmas Tree Safety — Water It Daily and Keep It Away From Heat
Description: Fire safety groups like NFPA say a dried-out Christmas tree can burn very quickly. Cut a little off the trunk before you put it in the stand, check the water every day and keep it full, and set the tree at least 3 feet from fireplaces, space heaters, vents and candles. Turn off the tree lights at bedtime and when you leave, and take the tree down once it's dry. More holiday safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: Read the Seller's Disclosure Before You Make an Offer
Description: In many states sellers fill out a disclosure form about the home's known problems: water, roof, repairs, permits and more. Ask for it early and read every line. Lots of "unknown" answers, past water or roof issues, or repairs without permits are worth asking about and pointing out to your home inspector. Rules vary by state, so ask your agent what applies. Title: Frost in the Attic? What It Means and What to Check
Description: On a cold morning, look into the attic from the hatch with a flashlight. Frost on the underside of the roof boards or white tips on the nails usually means warm, moist air from the house is leaking into the attic. Check that bath and kitchen fans vent outside, not into the attic, and ask an energy or insulation pro about air sealing. Don't walk on the ceiling joists. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Run Every Faucet at a House Showing — What to Watch For
Description: At a showing, turn on each faucet for a minute and flush the toilets. Watch for weak water pressure, slow or gurgling drains, rusty or cloudy water, and open the cabinet underneath to look for drips, stains or a soft floor. It's a quick, polite check, and anything odd is worth asking the seller about and pointing out to your home inspector. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: How to Prevent Ice Dams — Causes, Warning Signs and Safe Fixes
Description: Thick icicles and a ridge of ice along the roof edge can mean an ice dam. Heat and warm air leaking into the attic melt the snow on the roof, and the water refreezes at the cold eaves, where it can back up under the shingles. Look from the ground, stay off icy roofs, and watch ceilings near outside walls for stains. Air sealing and insulation are the long-term fix. Read Walter's full guide to preventing ice dams.

Title: Check Your Stove's Anti-Tip Bracket (Kitchen Safety for Families)
Description: The CPSC warns that freestanding ranges can tip forward if someone, often a child, climbs or stands on the open oven door. An anti-tip bracket holds the range in place. Check your range manual for how to tell if one is installed, or ask the installer to check. Many new ranges come with one in the box. A quick kitchen safety check before the holiday cooking. Title: Sloping Floors at a Showing — When to Ask More Questions
Description: Walk each room slowly at a showing. A floor you can feel tilt or bounce, especially with diagonal wall cracks, doors that stick or gaps under baseboards nearby, is worth a closer look. Some settling is common in older houses, but your home inspector may suggest a structural engineer if the slope is noticeable. Ask the seller if anything was repaired. Title: Holiday Candle Safety — Keep Them a Foot Away From Anything That Burns
Description: NFPA advises keeping candles at least 12 inches from anything that can burn, like curtains, holiday decorations, wrapping paper and the tree. Use sturdy holders on a flat surface, keep them out of reach of kids and pets, and blow them out when you leave the room or go to bed. Battery candles give the same glow without the flame. More holiday safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: Anchor Your TV and Furniture — A Simple Child Safety Check
Description: The CPSC warns that TVs, dressers and bookcases can tip over onto young children. If you're setting up a new TV for the holidays, mount it or anchor it with an anti-tip strap, and anchor dressers and bookcases to the wall. Keep remotes and toys off high furniture so kids aren't tempted to climb. A small home job with a big safety payoff. More safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: New Carpet Only in the Basement — What to Ask Before You Buy
Description: Brand-new carpet in a finished basement can be a nice update, or it can be covering up past water. Look at the bottom of the walls for stains, peeling paint or a white chalky powder, notice any musty smell, and look at the corners near the floor. Ask the seller directly if the basement has ever had water, and when the carpet went in. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: Clay Sewer Pipes in Older Homes — Why a Camera Inspection Helps
Description: Many older homes have a sewer line made of clay pipe sections. Over the years, tree roots can find their way into the joints, and pipes can crack or sag. Slow drains in the lowest part of the house or gurgling toilets can be early signs. Buying an older home? Ask about a sewer camera inspection by a plumber before you close. More older home checks on Walter's free house-age tool.

Title: After a Snowstorm, Clear Snow From Your Dryer Vent Outside
Description: After a big snowfall, find where your dryer vents outside and make sure the flap isn't buried or iced shut. A blocked vent keeps hot, moist air and lint in the duct, and with a gas dryer, exhaust can back up into the house. Clear the snow gently by hand, check the other vents on that wall too, and make sure your CO alarms work. More winter home prep on Walter's page.
Keywords: dryer vent snow, winter home maintenance, carbon monoxide safety, snow blocked vent, winter home prep, homeowner tips

Title: Check Your Garage Door Bottom Seal Before Winter
Description: Close the garage door and look along the bottom from inside, ideally on a sunny day. If you see daylight, a cracked or flattened rubber seal, or gaps at the corners, cold air, snow, water and mice can get in. Many bottom seals can be replaced as a simple project; for the springs, cables and opener, call a garage door pro. More easy home checks on Walter's page.

Title: Look at the Furnace Filter at a Showing — A Small Clue That Says a Lot
Description: At a showing, find the furnace or air handler and look at the filter if it's easy to see. A filter caked with dust can hint that regular maintenance was skipped. Ask the seller how old the furnace and AC are, when they were last serviced, and for any records. Your home inspector will look at the system, and you can ask about an HVAC check too. Title: Older Uncoated Brass Gas Connectors — Have a Pro Take a Look
Description: The CPSC has warned that some older uncoated brass flexible gas connectors, the tubes that link a gas stove, dryer or water heater to the gas line, can crack or come apart. If your home is older and the appliances have never been replaced, ask a qualified gas technician or plumber to check the connectors. Don't move or bend them yourself. If you smell gas, get out and call the gas company. More older home checks on Walter's free tool.
Keywords: gas connector, brass gas connector, older home safety, gas appliance safety, older homes, homeowner tips

Title: 5 House Checks After a Winter Storm
Description: After a winter storm, walk around the house from the ground: clear snow from furnace, water heater and dryer vents, look up at the roof and gutters for heavy snow or big icicles, check ceilings and walls near outside walls for new stains, and keep well away from any downed power lines and call the utility. Stay off icy roofs. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Pipes in the Garage? Keep the Garage Door Closed in a Freeze
Description: Many homes have water lines in the garage or in the wall between the garage and the house, and sometimes a water heater or laundry too. When it's very cold, keep the big garage door closed as much as you can so those pipes don't freeze. Look for pipes on outside walls and ask a plumber about insulating them. Keep the main water shutoff easy to reach. More winter home prep on Walter's page.
Keywords: garage pipes freezing, prevent frozen pipes, winter home prep, cold garage, frozen pipes, homeowner tips

Title: Condensation on Windows in Winter — What's Normal and What to Do
Description: Water or frost on the inside of your windows on cold mornings usually means humid indoor air is meeting cold glass. Run bath and kitchen fans, open the curtains during the day, and keep an eye on indoor humidity; the EPA suggests ideally 30 to 50 percent. Fog between the panes means a failed seal. Water on the sills or black spots are worth a closer look. Read Walter's full guide to window condensation.

Title: Buying a House During the Holidays — Look Behind the Decorations
Description: A house dressed for the holidays looks great, and that's the point. But big trees, rugs, garlands and furniture moved for decorations can block walls, floors, outlets and windows. Politely ask to see behind them, look at ceilings and corners, and make sure your home inspector can reach everything. Ask for photos without the decor too. More buyer tips on Walter's page.

Title: Older Home With No Bathroom Fan? Watch for Winter Moisture
Description: Many older homes were built with only a window in the bathroom, no exhaust fan. In winter nobody opens it, so shower steam stays in the room: look for peeling paint, black spots on the ceiling or a musty smell. Ask an electrician or contractor about adding a fan that vents outside, not into the attic. Older paint can contain lead, so don't sand it. More older home checks on Walter's free house-age tool.
Keywords: bathroom exhaust fan, bathroom moisture, older home problems, mold prevention, older homes, winter home tips

Title: 5 Places to Check for Hidden Leaks This Winter
Description: Once a month this winter, take a flashlight and check for drips, stains and damp spots under sinks on outside walls, around the water heater, behind the washing machine, in the attic near the chimney and vents, and on ceilings below bathrooms. Small leaks are easier to catch early. Find something wet? Turn off the water to it if you can and call a plumber. More easy home checks on Walter's page.
